The insula group was more likely to have a disruption of smoking addiction: they quit easily, immediately and without relapse or a persisting urge to smoke. The damage covered the insula broadly and was not limited to the anterior part.
evidence.quote: We found that smokers with brain damage involving the insula, a region implicated in conscious urges, were more likely than smokers with brain damage not involving the insula to undergo a disruption of smoking addiction, characterized by the ability to quit smoking easily, immediately, without relapse, and without persistence of the urge to smoke.
evidence.cite: Naqvi NH, Rudrauf D, Damasio H, Bechara A. Damage to the insula disrupts addiction to cigarette smoking. Science. 2007;315(5811):531-4.

evidence.claim: Stimulating the anteroventral insula evokes smell sensations
evidence.finding: Intracranial electrical stimulation was applied across the brain in 302 neurosurgical patients with epilepsy. Chemosensory perceptions were evoked in 7% of patients and 0.2% of stimulated sites, with the highest response rate, 1.8%, in the insula. The anteroventral insula mostly produced orthonasal smell and the mid-dorsal insula produced several chemosensory modalities.
evidence.quote: The chemosensory perceptions including olfaction, gustation, and chemesthesis were elicited in 21 of 302 patients (7%). Chemosensory responses were evoked in 53 (0.2%) of 21,661 stimulated sites. The highest response rate (1.8%) was in the insula (37/2,051 stimulated sites from 15/163 patients).
evidence.cite: Li Y, Tan Z, Wang J, et al. Responses of chemosensory perception to stimulation of the human brain. Ann Neurol. 2023;93(1):175-183.

data.title: Percent of patients or sites with a chemosensory response

stimulation.method: intracranial electrical stimulation in epilepsy patients
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the anteroventral insula predominantly produced the sensation of smell through the nose, and the mid-dorsal insula produced several chemosensory sensations, but responses were rare overall.
stimulation.quote: Notably, there existed a distinct pattern that the anteroventral insula predominately represented orthonasal olfaction, whereas different chemosensory modalities converged in the mid-dorsal insula.
stimulation.cite: Li Y, Tan Z, Wang J, et al. Responses of chemosensory perception to stimulation of the human brain. Ann Neurol. 2023;93(1):175-183.

hint: back of the buried island, behind its central sulcus, under the lid
summary: The posterior insula is the rear, granular part of the insular cortex, buried in the lateral sulcus beneath the parietal and temporal opercula. It receives touch, temperature, pain and visceral information from the thalamus and passes it forward to the mid and anterior insula. Direct electrical stimulation here can evoke pain and other body sensations. It is considered a primary cortex for interoception and for the sensory side of pain.
where: It lies in the depths of the lateral sulcus, behind the central sulcus of the insula, on the long insular gyri, and is covered by the parietal operculum above and the temporal operculum below. It is best seen with the opercula faded or in a lateral view of the insula. It is drawn from HCP areas Ig, PoI1 and PoI2, so the outline is approximate, and it borders the parietal operculum (secondary somatosensory cortex).
does: The posterior insula encodes the physical qualities of body signals: touch, innocuous warmth and cooling, pain, itch and visceral sensation. Direct electrical stimulation in epilepsy patients shows it is one of the only cortical sites that can evoke pain, along with the medial parietal operculum next to it, and a rough body map exists with the face represented in front of the arm and leg. It is more concerned with the sensory-discriminative side of pain than the anterior insula, which handles how unpleasant it is. A dorsal posterior sector is proposed to be specific to pain.
connects: It receives nociceptive, thermal and visceral input from the posterior and ventromedial thalamic nuclei, and from the adjacent parietal operculum. It sends information forward to the mid and anterior insula, and to the amygdala and cingulate cortex.
clinical: Insular strokes can cause central poststroke pain and altered pain or temperature sensation on the opposite side, and in pain asymbolia insular damage leaves pain recognized but not distressing. Seizures arising in the posterior insula often start with painful or tingling body sensations and are mistaken for parietal seizures. Stimulation of this region is a diagnostic tool in epilepsy surgery.
remember: The posterior insula is the body's sensor panel: it logs what the sensation is (hot, sharp, touch) before the anterior insula decides how it feels.
facts: Direct stimulation of the posterior insula and medial parietal operculum can evoke pain.
Stimulation-evoked pain in the insula shows a rough body map, with the face in front of the arm and leg.
The granular posterior insula is the sensory-discriminative end of the posterior-to-anterior insular gradient.

quiz.q: Which buried cortex behind the central sulcus of the insula can evoke pain when stimulated electrically in epilepsy patients?
Epilepsy patients with depth electrodes reported painful sensations in the face, arm or leg when this region was stimulated. Which region?
Which part of the insula is granular, lies on the long insular gyri behind the central insular sulcus, and borders the parietal operculum?

how_we_know: Direct stimulation shows causally which sites can produce pain and other sensations, and fMRI shows which sub-regions respond to which stimulus type. Stimulation only reaches the places where electrodes happen to be placed in epilepsy patients, and pain responses are rare, so the evidence is strong for a role in pain but gives a rough map.

evidence.claim: Stimulating the posterior insula evokes pain and other body sensations
evidence.finding: Direct electrical stimulation of the insular cortex was done in 43 patients with drug-refractory temporal lobe epilepsy, using depth electrodes. Painful sensations arose in the upper posterior insula in 14 patients, mostly in the right hemisphere, and non-painful sensations arose in the posterior insula in 16 patients in both hemispheres. The two kinds of representation overlapped.
evidence.quote: We studied painful and non-painful somaesthetic sensations elicited by direct electrical stimulations of the insular cortex performed in 43 patients with drug refractory temporal lobe epilepsy, using stereotactically implanted depth electrodes. Painful sensations were evoked in the upper posterior part of the insular cortex in 14 patients, mostly in the right hemisphere. Non-painful sensations were elicited in the posterior part of the insular cortex in 16 patients, in both hemispheres.
evidence.cite: Ostrowsky K, Magnin M, Ryvlin P, et al. Representation of pain and somatic sensation in the human insula: a study of responses to direct electrical cortical stimulation. Cereb Cortex. 2002;12(4):376-85.

data.title: Patients (of 43) with sensations from insular stimulation

evidence.claim: Pain from insular stimulation has a rough body map, mostly posterior
evidence.finding: In 142 patients having depth electrode exploration, 472 insular stimulations were delivered. Only 10.5% elicited pain, in 27% of patients, and most sites were in the posterior two thirds of the insula. Pain sites showed a face representation in front of the upper limb, with the upper limb above the lower limb.
evidence.quote: We studied 142 patients undergoing depth stereotactic EEG (SEEG) exploration of the insular cortex for pre-surgical evaluation of epilepsy. 472 insular electrical stimulations were delivered, of which only 49 (10.5%) elicited a painful sensation in 38 patients (27%).
evidence.cite: Mazzola L, Isnard J, Peyron R, Guenot M, Mauguiere F. Somatotopic organization of pain responses to direct electrical stimulation of the human insular cortex. Pain. 2009;146(1-2):99-104.

evidence.claim: The granular posterior insula responds specifically to pain stimuli
evidence.finding: In 25 healthy volunteers, tactile stimuli, passive movements, cold, warmth and heat pain were applied to the left hand during fMRI. The posterior granular insula (Ig) and the anterior parietal operculum (OP4) were specifically activated by pain, which raises the question of whether they are the substrate of sensory-discriminative processing of thermal pain.
evidence.quote: However, the posterior granular part of insula contralateral to stimulus (Ig area) and the anterior part of SII bilaterally (OP4) were specifically activated during pain stimulation.
evidence.cite: Mazzola L, Faillenot I, Barral FG, Mauguiere F, Peyron R. Spatial segregation of somato-sensory and pain activations in the human operculo-insular cortex. Neuroimage. 2012;60(1):409-18.

evidence.claim: The dorsal posterior insula has a specific role in pain
evidence.finding: The authors used arterial spin-labeling perfusion imaging and a new analysis procedure to look for a pain-specific region. They identified the dorsal posterior insula as having a specific role in pain, similar to a region that animal tracing studies place at the center of nociception.
evidence.quote: We exploited arterial spin-labeling quantitative perfusion imaging and a newly developed procedure to identify a specific role for the dorsal posterior insula (dpIns) in pain.
evidence.cite: Segerdahl AR, Mezue M, Okell TW, Farrar JT, Tracey I. The dorsal posterior insula subserves a fundamental role in human pain. Nat Neurosci. 2015;18(4):499-500.

stimulation.method: intracerebral electrical stimulation in epilepsy patients
stimulation.effect: In 164 consecutive patients and 4160 stimulations, pain was rare but arose from the medial parietal operculum and neighbouring posterior insula, and nowhere else in the cortex.
stimulation.quote: Pain responses were scarce (1.4%) and concentrated in the medial part of the parietal operculum and neighbouring posterior insula where pain thresholds showed a rostrocaudal decrement.
stimulation.cite: Mazzola L, Isnard J, Peyron R, Mauguiere F. Stimulation of the human cortex and the experience of pain: Wilder Penfield's observations revisited. Brain. 2012;135(Pt 2):631-40.

hint: underside where the smell tract ends, at the frontotemporal border
summary: The piriform cortex is the main primary olfactory cortex, a three-layered paleocortex at the junction of the frontal and temporal lobes. It receives smell information directly from the olfactory bulb through the lateral olfactory tract, without a thalamic relay. It encodes odor quality as distributed patterns of activity, and its posterior part appears to hold templates of odor identity. It projects to the orbitofrontal cortex, amygdala, entorhinal cortex and hippocampus, which link smell to emotion and memory.
where: It lies on the ventral surface of the brain at the border between the frontal and temporal lobes, where the lateral olfactory tract ends, around the limen insulae and in front of and around the amygdala at the uncus. It is a small structure on the underside of the hemisphere, best seen in an inferior view. The frontal part sits in the posterior orbitofrontal area, and the temporal part lies around the uncus.
does: The piriform cortex builds odor objects: patterns of activity across it correspond to perceived odor quality, particularly in the posterior piriform cortex, where more similar patterns match odors that are rated as more similar. The anterior part reflects the attended odor target before and after the odor arrives, and the posterior part shifts from a prestimulus template to the odor itself. It responds to sniffing as well as to smell, and takes part in recognition memory for odors and in linking odors to other senses.
connects: The mitral and tufted cells of the olfactory bulb project to it directly through the lateral olfactory tract, so olfaction is the one sense that reaches cortex without first synapsing in the thalamus. It projects to the orbitofrontal cortex, directly and through the mediodorsal thalamus, and to the amygdala, entorhinal cortex, hippocampus and insula.
clinical: Smell loss is an early feature of Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease, whose pathology involves the olfactory bulb, piriform and entorhinal regions. Seizures that start in the medial temporal lobe near the uncus can begin with a brief unpleasant smell, called an uncinate fit. Removing the temporal lobe or orbital frontal cortex impairs odor identification in patients, but detection thresholds stay normal.
remember: Piriform means pear-shaped: it is the first cortical stop for smell, reached straight from the nose-side bulb with no thalamic relay.
facts: Olfaction is the only sense that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay.
Posterior piriform activity patterns coincide with perceived odor similarity.
Sniffing alone, without a smell, activates the piriform cortex.

quiz.q: Which paleocortex at the frontotemporal junction receives mitral cell axons from the olfactory bulb directly, without a thalamic relay?
In fMRI, activity patterns in this posterior cortex match how similar odors smell. Which region?
Temporal lobe seizures near the uncus start with a brief unpleasant smell, and smell loss is an early sign of Parkinson's disease. Which primary olfactory cortex is involved?

how_we_know: Most of what we know is from fMRI in healthy volunteers, which shows what odor information piriform patterns hold but not what they are needed for, and from lesion studies that include more than the piriform cortex. Direct human stimulation evidence that targets the piriform cortex specifically is thin, so no stimulation result is given here.

evidence.claim: Posterior piriform patterns track perceived odor similarity
evidence.finding: Volunteers smelled a range of odors during fMRI, and pattern analysis was used to compare the activity with their ratings of odor quality. Distributed activity in the human posterior piriform cortex coincided with perceived odor quality, so that odors with more similar patterns were perceived as more alike. This was not seen in the anterior piriform cortex, the amygdala or the orbitofrontal cortex. It is correlational.
evidence.quote: By combining functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with multivariate (pattern-based) techniques, we found that spatially distributed ensemble activity in human posterior piriform cortex (PPC) coincides with perceptual ratings of odor quality, such that odorants with more (or less) similar fMRI patterns were perceived as more (or less) alike.
evidence.cite: Howard JD, Plailly J, Grueschow M, Haynes JD, Gottfried JA. Odor quality coding and categorization in human posterior piriform cortex. Nat Neurosci. 2009;12(7):932-8.

evidence.claim: Anterior and posterior piriform cortex hold odor target templates
evidence.finding: Using high-resolution fMRI during an odor search task, the authors found that anterior piriform cortex and orbitofrontal cortex patterns reflected the attended odor target both before and after stimulus onset. In the posterior piriform cortex, prestimulus patterns for the target gave way to patterns for the odor itself, and the strength of the target pattern predicted later performance.
evidence.quote: Ensemble activity patterns in anterior piriform cortex (APC) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) reflected the attended odor target both before and after stimulus onset. In contrast, prestimulus ensemble representations of the odor target in posterior piriform cortex (PPC) gave way to poststimulus representations of the odor itself.
evidence.cite: Zelano C, Mohanty A, Gottfried JA. Olfactory predictive codes and stimulus templates in piriform cortex. Neuron. 2011;72(1):178-87.

evidence.claim: Sniffing activates the piriform cortex even without an odor
evidence.finding: fMRI in healthy volunteers separated sniffing from smelling. Sniffing, with or without an odorant, activated mainly the piriform cortex and the medial and posterior orbitofrontal gyri, while a smell regardless of sniffing activated mainly the lateral and anterior orbitofrontal gyri. The sniff response came from the somatosensory stimulation of air flow through the nostrils.
evidence.quote: We find that sniffing, whether odorant is present or absent, induces activation primarily in the piriform cortex of the temporal lobe and in the medial and posterior orbito-frontal gyri of the frontal lobe. In contrast, a smell, regardless of sniffing, induces activation mainly in the lateral and anterior orbito-frontal gyri of the frontal lobe.
evidence.cite: Sobel N, Prabhakaran V, Desmond JE, et al. Sniffing and smelling: separate subsystems in the human olfactory cortex. Nature. 1998;392(6673):282-6.

evidence.claim: Temporal or orbital frontal removal impairs odor identification
evidence.finding: The University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test was given to 120 patients with a focal surgical lesion and 20 control subjects. Identification was significantly impaired after temporal lobectomy, which removes the piriform cortex among other tissue, and after frontal lobectomy that invaded the orbital cortex. Detection thresholds were normal, and the lesions were not confined to the piriform cortex.
evidence.quote: The ability to identify common odors using the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test was investigated in 120 patients with a focal surgical brain lesion and 20 normal control subjects. Results showed significant impairment after right or left temporal lobectomy, right or left frontal lobectomy, and right frontotemporal excision.
evidence.cite: Jones-Gotman M, Zatorre RJ. Olfactory identification deficits in patients with focal cerebral excision. Neuropsychologia. 1988;26(3):387-400.

hint: upper lip and bank of the lateral sulcus, behind the insular island
summary: The secondary somatosensory cortex is the part of the somatosensory system on the parietal operculum, the upper bank of the lateral sulcus, behind the insula and below the primary somatosensory cortex. It receives touch, temperature and pain information from the primary somatosensory cortex and the thalamus, and has large receptive fields that often cover both sides of the body. It integrates touch for recognising objects and takes part in the sensory side of pain and in attention to touch. It projects to the posterior insula and, from there, to limbic structures that store tactile memories.
where: It lies on the parietal operculum, the upper bank and lip of the lateral sulcus, directly behind the posterior insula and below the lower end of the postcentral gyrus. It is best seen in a lateral view with the lateral sulcus opened. The model draws it from HCP areas OP1, OP2-3 and OP4, so the outline is an approximation of S2 that also includes neighbouring operculum fields.
does: The secondary somatosensory cortex processes touch at a higher level than the primary cortex. It combines inputs from many skin regions, so a single finger can activate wide areas on both sides, and it helps recognise objects by touch. It has a coarse body map that is less detailed than the primary cortex. Subdivisions differ: OP1 resembles the human equivalent of S2 and is closely tied to parietal networks for higher-order touch, while OP4 is tied more to frontal motor and action-control areas.
connects: It receives input from the primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3b, 1 and 2) and from thalamic nuclei, and projects to the posterior insula, the premotor and motor areas and the parietal association cortex. Anatomical and functional connectivity analyses show OP1 is more closely connected to parietal networks and OP4 to frontal motor areas.
clinical: Damage to the parietal operculum and adjacent parietal cortex can cause tactile agnosia, in which a patient cannot recognise an object by touch even though basic sensation is preserved. Stimulation of its medial part, together with the posterior insula, can evoke pain. Operculo-insular lesions can also alter pain and temperature sensation, whereas stimulation of the lateral part of S2 did not evoke pain.
remember: S2 is the second stop for touch: S1 says where and what kind, S2 pools both sides of the body to say what the object is.
facts: S2 lies on the parietal operculum, the upper bank of the lateral sulcus.
Its receptive fields are often bilateral and its body map is coarser than S1.
OP1 is more connected to parietal networks, and OP4 to frontal motor and action areas.

quiz.q: Which area on the upper bank of the lateral sulcus has bilateral receptive fields and helps recognise objects by touch?
A patient can feel light touch normally but cannot recognise a coin placed in the hand without looking. Damage to which opercular region is suspected?
Which somatosensory cortex lies on the parietal operculum behind the insula, with subdivisions OP1 and OP4?

how_we_know: fMRI shows a coarse body map and separate subdivisions, tractography shows the connection pattern, and intracerebral stimulation shows where stimulation does and does not give pain. S2 sits deep in the sulcus next to the insula, so separating it from the posterior insula is hard and the boundaries on the model are approximate.

evidence.claim: S2 has a coarse body map that is also found in the ipsilateral side
evidence.finding: Eight subjects had electrical stimulation of the second finger, the fifth finger and the hallux during fMRI. Both fingers were represented halfway down the contralateral parietal operculum, and the hallux more medially near the posterior pole of the insula. Separate finger representations were not seen, so the S2 map is coarser than the S1 map.
evidence.quote: Eight subjects received electrical stimulation on their right second finger, fifth finger and hallux. Within SII, the typical finding for both fingers was a representation site within the contralateral parietal operculum roughly halfway between the lip of the lateral sulcus and its fundus, whereas the representation site of the hallux was found more medially to this position at the fundus of the lateral sulcus, near the posterior pole of the insula.
evidence.cite: Ruben J, Schwiemann J, Deuchert M, et al. Somatotopic organization of human secondary somatosensory cortex. Cereb Cortex. 2001;11(5):463-73.

evidence.claim: OP1 links to parietal networks and OP4 to frontal motor areas
evidence.finding: Probabilistic tractography on diffusion data and a coordinate-based meta-analysis of functional imaging were used to compare the connectivity of the two largest parietal operculum areas. OP4 was more closely integrated with areas for basic sensorimotor processing and action control, while OP1 was more closely connected to the parietal networks for higher-order somatosensory processing.
evidence.quote: In particular, relative to OP 1, area OP 4 is more closely integrated with areas responsible for basic sensorimotor processing and action control, while OP 1 is more closely connected to the parietal networks for higher order somatosensory processing.
evidence.cite: Eickhoff SB, Jbabdi S, Caspers S, et al. Anatomical and functional connectivity of cytoarchitectonic areas within the human parietal operculum. J Neurosci. 2010;30(18):6409-21.

evidence.claim: OP1 responds to every type of touch stimulus and OP4 to pain
evidence.finding: In 25 healthy volunteers, five kinds of somatosensory stimulus (tactile, passive movement, cold, warmth and heat pain) were applied to the left hand during fMRI. The posterior part of S2 (OP1) was the only subregion activated by all stimulus types, while the anterior part (OP4) was specifically activated by pain.
evidence.quote: The posterior part of SII (OP1 area), contralateral to stimuli, was the only sub-region activated by all type of stimuli and might therefore be considered as a common cortical target for different types of somato-sensory inputs.
evidence.cite: Mazzola L, Faillenot I, Barral FG, Mauguiere F, Peyron R. Spatial segregation of somato-sensory and pain activations in the human operculo-insular cortex. Neuroimage. 2012;60(1):409-18.

stimulation.method: intracerebral electrical stimulation in epilepsy patients
stimulation.effect: Across 4160 stimulations in 164 patients, pain was evoked from the medial parietal operculum and neighbouring posterior insula, but no pain response occurred from the lateral part of the secondary somatosensory area.
stimulation.quote: Like Penfield et al., we obtained no pain response anywhere else in the cortex, including in regions consistently activated by pain in most functional imaging studies, i.e. the first somatosensory area, the lateral part of the secondary somatosensory area, anterior and mid-cingulate gyri (mid-cingulate cortex), anterior frontal, posterior parietal and supplementary motor areas.
stimulation.cite: Mazzola L, Isnard J, Peyron R, Mauguiere F. Stimulation of the human cortex and the experience of pain: Wilder Penfield's observations revisited. Brain. 2012;135(Pt 2):631-40.
